JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present appeal has been filed by Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited
(“Appellant”) challenging the Order dated 29.03.2016 (“Impugned Order”)
passed by the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred as “State Commission/CSERC”), in Petition No. 56 of
2012(M).
Description of Parties: -
2. The Appellant, Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited (earlier know as Lafarge
India Limited) Sonadih Cement Plant is a Limited Company incorporated under
Companies Act 1956 engaged in production of cement.
Page 2 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
3. The Respondent No.1/CSERC is the State Regulatory Commission for the
State of Chhattisgarh, discharging statutory functions in terms of Electricity Act
2003. Respondent No. 2, the Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Company
Limited ("CSPDCL") is the State Distribution Company.
Factual matrix of the Case:
4. The Appellant, a manufacturer of cement, is a captive user of power
generated by its own joint venture company, Arasmeta Captive Power Company
Private Limited ("ACCPL"), which operates a 43 MW coal-based captive power
plant at village Arasmeta, District Janjgir-Champa, running in parallel with the
distribution system of Respondent for making use of the power of the plant for its
cement plants at Sonadih, District- Raipur and the cement plant at village
Arasmeta, District Champa- Jangir. Permission for parallel operation of the
captive plant, and separately for wheeling of 16 MW of power from ACCPL to the
Appellant's Sonadih cement plant through open access, was granted by CSPDCL
vide its letters dated 11.11.2005.
5. Vide order dated 06.02.2006 in Petition No. 17 of 2005(M), the State
Commission made certain special dispensations to promote captive generation,
including a relaxation for captive consumers. On review of the same, by order
dated 29.09.2006 in Petition No. 16 of 2006(M), the State Commission liberalised
this dispensation further, granting captive consumers a liberty to reduce their
contract demand to any extent even to zero at any time during the entire period
of the two years of the HT agreement and to avail standby power from the
licensee, subject to exemption from tariff minimum charges.
Page 3 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
6. Acting on this dispensation, the Appellant, by its letter dated 10.10.2006,
applied to Respondent No 2-CSPDCL for reduction of its contract demand to zero
with effect from 16.10.2006. CSPDCL, by letter dated 04.11.2006, declined to
give effect to the reduction from the date sought, invoking Clause 7.11 of the
Chhattisgarh State Electricity Supply Code, 2005 ("the Supply Code"), and
informed the Appellant that the request was under process.
7. Vide its letter dated 15.12.2006, CSPDCL permitted reduction of contract
demand to zero, with effect from 01.01.2007. For the period 4.11.2006 to
31.12.2006, the Respondent presumed that the Appellant was allowed to wheel
16MW of power from its captive plant at Arasmeta but was also to be having a
contract demand of 9500 KVA with the licensee.
8. The Respondent-CSPDCL issued energy bills of the months October 2006
(16.10.2006 to 15.11.2006), November 2006 (16.11.2006 to 15.12.2006) and
January 2007 (for the period 16.12.2006 to 15.01.2007).
9. Aggrieved by the billing for the period (4.11.2006 to 31.12.2006) in question,
the Appellant addressed a series of letters to CSPDCL between November 2006
and February 2007, and thereafter periodically until 2012, principally raising
discrepancies concerning wheeled units, electricity duty and cess. The dispute
concerning electricity duty was resolved in December 2011 following
correspondence with the Chief Electrical Inspector, Government of Chhattisgarh.
However, by letter dated 18.05.2012, CSPDCL's Managing Director informed the
Appellant, that the billing had been carried out in accordance with the prevailing
rules.
Page 4 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
10. The Appellant thereupon filed Petition No. 56 of 2012(M) before the State
Commission raising the dispute from 04.10.2006 to 31.12.2006 which was initially
dismissed vide order dated 12.03.2013 on the ground of limitation. On appeal
(Appeal No. 127 of 2013), a Full Bench of this Tribunal held, by order dated
13.03.2015, held that the Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply to proceedings
before State/Central Electricity Regulatory Commissions and remanded the
matter. The State Commission challenged this ruling before the Hon'ble Supreme
Court (Civil Appeal Nos. 5336-5337 of 2015), which was disposed of on
20.07.2015 with a direction that the State Commission decide the matter on
merits. Pursuant thereto, the petition was heard afresh and State Commission
dismissed the said petition filed by the Appellant seeking, inter alia, a refund of
Rs. 1,40,96,072/- allegedly overcharged by Respondent No. 2 - CSPDCL.
Aggrieved by such finding, Appellant has filed present Appeal contending that for
the period from 04.11.2006 to 31.12.2006, the Respondent –CSPDCL created an
anomalous and legally untenable situation, i.e. while permitting the Appellant to
wheel 16 MW Electricity from its generating plant, the CSPDCL simultaneously
treated the Appellant as continuing to have a contract demand of 9500 KVA,
which resulted in wrongful and excessive billing of Rs. 1,40,96,072 and sought
refund of the same along with interest.
DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
11. Heard Mr. Gaurav Bahl, learned counsel for the Appellant, Ms. Rupinder
Kaur Learned Counsel for the Respondent No 1, Mr. Akhil Hasija, Learned
Counsel for the Respondent No 2, perused the written submissions filed by the
parties, Impugned Order and other documents. The summary of the submissions
made by parties and our consideration are deliberated in following paragraphs:
Page 5 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT
12. The Learned Counsel for the Appellant submits that the State Commission
vide its order dated 06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006 relaxed the restrictions for
captive consumers, permitting reduction of Contract Demand to any extent,
including zero, at any time during the currency of the agreement. Therefore, the
Clause 7.9 of the Supply Code which restricts the reduction of Contract Demand
during the initial period of supply, and Clause 7.11 which prescribes the procedure
for considering such applications stood altered by the Commission itself, and the
Respondent CSPDCL had no discretion to insist upon compliance with provisions
rendered inapplicable in this regard.
13. It is submitted that the Appellant, by its letter dated 10.10.2006, availed the
option to reduce its Contract Demand to zero with effect from 16.10.2006, and
sought standby power of 16 MW (17.78 MVA). By letter dated 04.11.2006,
CSPDCL declined to give effect to the reduction from the date sought, but on the
very same date permitted actual wheeling of 16 MW of electricity from ACCPL to
the Appellant's Sonadih Cement Plant as evidenced by the joint meter readings
recorded on 04.11.2006 and the communication dated 29.11.2006 issued by the
Chief Engineer (Commercial).
14. Having thus recognised and operationalised the Open Access
arrangement, the Respondent-CSPDCL could not simultaneously continue to
treat the Appellant as an ordinary HT consumer with a Contract Demand of 9500
KVA. Such a position is self-contradictory and contrary to the very scheme
contemplated under the Commission's orders dated 06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006,
and the Respondent's communication dated 04.11.2006 refusing to recognise the
Page 6 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
reduction was accordingly arbitrary, unreasonable and contrary to the regulatory
framework.
15. CSPDCL ultimately approved reduction of Contract Demand to zero only
with effect from 01.01.2007, vide its letter dated 15.12.2006, resulting in an
untenable billing situation for the intervening period from 04.11.2006 to
31.12.2006.
16. It is further submitted that the order dated 29.09.2006 obliged the
Respondent-CSPDCL to formulate and execute, after obtaining the
Commission's approval, a separate agreement distinct from the ordinary HT
agreement governing captive open access consumers opting for zero Contract
Demand while availing standby power. Admittedly, no such agreement was ever
executed, nor was even a draft furnished, despite the Appellant's repeated
requests. Having failed to comply with a mandatory requirement imposed upon it
by the Commission's order, the Respondent-CSPDCL could not subsequently
seek to impose liabilities inconsistent with the regulatory framework, and cannot
be permitted to take advantage of its own failure to comply with the Commission's
directions.
17. The Respondent raised bills for the periods 16.10.2006 to 15.11.2006
(October 2006), 16.11.2006 to 15.12.2006 (November 2006) and 16.12.2006 to
15.01.2007 (January 2007), ignoring the Appellant's reduction of Contract
Demand and thereby failing to account for: (a) the quantum of electricity wheeled
from the captive power plant; (b) the exemption from electricity duty and cess on
the wheeled units; and (c) the inapplicability of demand charges, penal demand
charges and minimum tariff charges under the Commission's regulatory
framework.
Page 7 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
18. Though the issue of electricity duty is now settled however Respondent-
CSPDCL, failed to rectify the bills insofar as demand charges, penal demand
charges, energy charges and penal energy charges are concerned. Its billing
methodology was erroneous in three respects: (a) it continued to assume a
Contract Demand of 9500 KVA despite the Appellant's exercised option and the
wheeling of 16 MW (17.78 MVA) commencing 04.11.2006; (b) it levied penal
demand charges at 1.5 times the normal tariff whenever recorded demand
exceeded 9500 KVA, though the Appellant never exceeded its sanctioned Open
Access capacity of 17.78 MVA; and (c) having correctly deducted the wheeled
energy from total consumption, it wrongly presumed the balance corresponded
to the recorded maximum demand and bifurcated it into normal and 1.5-times-
penal components, without basis in the Commission's orders or the regulatory
framework. This resulted in excessive billing of Rs. 1,40,96,072/-, causing
substantial financial prejudice to the Appellant. The State Commission, while
passing the Impugned Order, effectively rewrote its own earlier orders by
importing conditions and restrictions which do not exist therein.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF RESPONDENTS
19. It is submitted that though the order dated 06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006
granted a special dispensation to captive consumer, permitting them to reduce
their contact demand with the licensee to any extent, even to zero, at any time
during the period of agreement, however, the expression “Any time" means liberty
to apply and it does not imply automatic reduction. It does not override the
provisions contained in the Supply Code and therefore to be read in the context
in which it is used. The expression "any time" only relaxed the consumer to seek
reduction even during the initial agreement and did not dispense with verification
Page 8 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
or eliminate metering and commercial compliances and also did not authorise
retrospective alteration of billing. The Respondents submit that the clauses 7.9
and 7.11 of the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (“Supply Code
2005”) is statutory and binds both licensee and consumer. The State Commission
orders and the Supply Code 2005 must be read harmoniously and not as
displacing one another.
20. It is submitted that time framework as contained in the clause 7.11 provides
60 days to decide after the application is made by the consumer. There is
fundamental difference between a right to make an application and right to obtain
automatic approval from date chosen by the consumer. The consumer, as
provided, is not the authority to determine its own Contract Demand and billing
liability. The consumer first has a right to apply and after that licensee must
examine and verify and then decide the request. Therefore, the application dated
10.10.2006 made by the Appellant was not self-operative. Further, it is submitted
that on 04.11.2006 i.e., 25th day from the Application, the decision to not allow
was communicated to the Appellant. This letter was received by the Appellant
without any objection or protest. They submit that once CSPDCL communicated
its decision in December 2006, Clause 7.11(c) made the reduction effective from
the first day of the following month, i.e., 01.01.2007 as a matter of law, and no
refund can follow from a premise contrary to the Supply Code.
21. The Appellant’s request for load reduction involved captive wheeling, open-
access accounting and standby power, requiring ABT/SEM-compliant metering
at both injection and drawal points for accurate energy accounting, scheduling,
deviation treatment and billing. It is submitted that the permission for parallel
operation and wheeling were conditional and contemplated ABT/ SEM metering,
communication/ data transfer and billing modalities. The prerequisite requirement
Page 9 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
of SEM installation as per the Regulation 18 of the CSERC (Intra-Open Access
in Chhattisgarh) Regulations, 2005. as mentioned in the regulatory orders. The
very order dated 06.02.2006 vide which the Appellant invokes for the liberty to
reduce the contract demand, expressly directed that “existing arrangement for
billing will continue till SEMs are installed.”
22. It is evident from Appellant’s letter dated 20.01.2007 that ABT meter at
Sonadih was installed only in December 2006, and Appellant duty was not limited
to the arranging the meters but includes the installation, testing, Commissioning
and integration of SEMs. Until metering and verification were complete, CSPDCL
was justified in continuing to bill under the subsisting arrangement.
23. It is contended by Respondent-CSPDCL that Wheeling and contract
demand are legally distinct. Wheeling concerns the flow and accounting of energy
from the captive source whereas the contract demand concerns the licensee's
obligation to keep capacity available to the consumer. CSPDCL could account for
wheeled units while billing on the subsisting 9500 KVA contract demand until
01.01.2007, particularly as the Appellant continued to seek 16 MW of standby
power throughout. Standby supply required system planning, commercial terms
and metering discipline and the same cannot be presumed to exist without the
prescribed process. It is submitted that the Contract demand did not become
zero before 01.01.2007, resultantly the refund claim of Rs. 1,40,96,072/-, being
founded solely on the rejected premise of reduction from 16.10.2006, collapses.
24. The Open access framework and Section 42(2) of the Electricity Act do
not override the Supply Code. Open Access governs use of the distribution
system, surcharge/cross subsidy and wheeling rights but does not rewrite the
effective date of reduction of contract demand. Further non-finalisation of a
Page 10 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
separate agreement cannot be turned into a ground for immediate financial
benefit. If any separate agreement or billing modality was required, that only
reinforces the position that the arrangement was not self-operative on
16.10.2006. The Appellant cannot rely on the conditional permissions for benefit
and simultaneously reject the conditions precedent to their operation.
25. It is further submitted that the series of letters sent to Respondent -CSPDCL
dated 25.11.2006, 30.11.2006, 23.12.2006, 30.12.2006, 10.01.2007, 20.01.2007,
24.01.2007, 31.01.2007, 17.10.2011 and 03.11.2011 were marked with objection
on discrepancy in billing, wheeling charges, duty and cess, payment refund but
nowhere was the issue of load reduction from 9500 KVA to zero was agitated by
the Appellant. Rather this objection for the very first-time was raised only in
Petition 56 of 2012.
26. The bills for the period October to December 2006 were raised by CSPDCL
on the basis of the contract demand of 9500 KVA then subsisting under the
license and the Tariff Order dated 13.09.2006, including additional charges for
demand recorded in excess of the contract demand in terms of paragraph 5.7.10
of the said Tariff Order. Accordingly, there is no infirmity in the Impugned Order
OUR CONSIDERATION:-
27. It is an admitted position that the Appellant, by its application dated
10.10.2006, sought reduction of the contracted demand from 9500 KVA to zero
with effect from 16.10.2006. The Respondent–CSPDCL, vide communication
dated 04.11.2006, declined to accede to the request with immediate effect, citing
the requirement of installation of ABT meters and the stipulations contained in
Clause 7.11 of the Supply Code, 2005. The Respondent-CSPDCL, however,
Page 11 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
indicated that the application was under consideration and that a decision would
be conveyed in due course. Subsequently, by letter dated 15.12.2006, CSPDCL
permitted reduction of the contracted demand to zero with effect from 01.01.2007,
subject to compliance with the conditions imposed by the State Commission in
its order dated 29.09.2006, including execution of a fresh agreement. It is not in
dispute that the contract demand was reduced to Zero w.e.f 01.01.2007.
28. Appellant is aggrieved by levy of contract demand charges of 9500 KVA
and other related charges for a period from 04.11.2006 till 31.12.2006, especially
when Appellant has exercised option and the wheeling of 16 MW (17.78 MVA)
commencing 04.11.2006. It is the contention of Appellant that concession of
reduction of contract demand to Zero at any time would mean that the time period
stipulated in clause 7.11 of Supply Code has stood altered by the Commission
itself. While the Respondent contends that the relaxation was confined to the
substantive restriction under Clause 7.9, and that the procedural discipline of
Clause 7.11 continued to govern.
29. The main issue therefore, pertains to whether the relaxation in reducing the
contract demand by captive user granted vide State Commission Order dated
06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006 would mean relaxation in the procedure and timeline
prescribed under clause 7.11 of Supply Code 2005. In this context it is apposite
to extract the relevant paragraph of the State Commission order dated
06.02.2006:
“ 6.7 The Commission feels that its decision not to allow set off on CD may not
pose as serious a problem as has been made out by the petitioner for the
following reasons. The relevance of CD is only in relation to the maximum
demand (MD) charges and/or to a minimum guaranteed consumption where
there is a nexus in the tariff between CD and minimum consumption. Of the
three kinds of consumers mentioned in para 6.1 above, who are concerned with
CD, the last two will have the benefit of the liberal regime for reduction of CD in
Page 12 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
the Supply Code. The Supply Code (clause 7.9) permits reduction in CD to the
extent of 50% by a consumer only once within the period of agreement which is
two years. Further liberalizing this provision, the Commission directs that the
captive and non-captive consumers of a CPP may reduce their CD to the extent
desired, on availing power supply from the. CPP, any time during the period of
the agreement and to any extent. However, such reduction shall be permitted
only once in a year. In case, CD is reduced to zero level to avail only standby
power from the Board/licensee, the charges will be tariff for temporary
connection to that consumer for the period during which power is availed from
the licensee, following the provisions of para 8.5.6 of the NTP. So far as the CPP
itself is concerned, it can avail of start-up power as per para 8 of this order”.
30. The State Commission in its review order dated 29.09.2006 (review of the
order dated 06.02.2006), indicated the charges/tariff applicable for such captive
users, who reduces their contract demand to Zero, but are required to draw power
from the licensee under emergency, confirming its earlier order that Captive user
can reduce their contract demand to zero.
31. The State Commission in the Impugned Order held that it is the clause 7.9
which stand relaxed in terms of State Commission’s modified order and
considering the time line specified in clause 7.11 of Supply code 2005, licensee
has not made any wrong in reducing the contract demand from 01 January 2007.
Relevant portion of the Impugned Order is extracted hereunder:
“26. So far it concerns with clause 7.9, it is clear that the clause is relaxed in
case of captive user, by the modified order.
27. The clause 7.11 provides 60 daystime for taking decision, in case
reduction of contract demand sought. In the modified order it is provided that
a captive user can reduce it's contract demand even up to zero at any time
including the two years initial period, but in that order no time limit fixed for
the licensee for deciding the application. The expression "any time" used in
modified order does not mean immediate after making request.
28. It is desired that the application must be decided as early as possible,
but not beyond the period specified in the supply code. The narration used
"any time" shall mean accordingly. It is further to be considered that after
reduction of contract demand the licensee has to manage the balance load
Page 13 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
elsewhere, for which, it has needed some time. The time limit prescribed in
the supply. code seems reasonable. Hence, we arrive at a conclusion that the
licensee has not made any wrong by reducing the contract demand from 01
January, 2007”.
32. Since, the issue pertains to relaxation of Clause 7.9 and applicability of
Clause 7.11 of Supply code 2005, it is of relevance to extract the relevant clauses
of Supply Code 2005 as under:
Clause 7.9
“Generally no application for reduction of contract demand / connected load
shall be entertained by the licensee within the initial period of agreement,
which is two years from the date of commencement of contract. However, if
the consumer is able to satisfy the licensee of the compelling reasons for
reduction in contract demand/connected load, reduction to the extent of 50
percent of the contract demand/connected load shall be permitted once
during the period of agreement."
Clause 7.11
" On Receipt of the application for reduction of load, the licensee shall take
the following steps”
a) the licensee shall consider the grounds stated in the application. verify the
same and decide the application within a period of 60 days by a reasoned
speaking order. If the consumer is not satisfied with the decision of the
licensee, an appeal can be made to the Electricity Grievance Redressal
Forum set up by the licensee under Section 42 (5) of the Act and then to the
Electricity Ombudsman as appointed or designated by the Commission under
section 42 (6) of the Act whose decision shall be final subject to such remedy
as may be available under any statute.
(b) If the application is not decided by the licensee within the above-
mentioned period of 60 days, the applicant may, by a written notice, draw
attention to the matter and if no decision is still communicated to him within
the period of further 30 days, the permission of reduction of contract shall be
deemed to have been granted. the reduction of contract demand shall take
effect from the first day of the month following the month in which the decision
is communicated or permission is deemed to have been granted.
Page 14 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
(c) the reduction of contract demand shall take effect from the first day of the
month following the month in which the decision is communicated or
permission is deemed to have been granted."
33. A plain reading of Clause 7.9 of the Supply Code, 2005 discloses two
substantive restrictions: i) that reduction in contract demand within the initial
two-year period of agreement is ordinarily impermissible; and ii) however for
compelling reason, subject to satisfaction of licensee, reduction in contract
demand to the extent of 50 % is permitted that too only once during the period of
agreement i.e., once in two years. The clause also contains a separate stipulation
for domestic light and fan consumers, which is not germane to the present
controversy.
34. The State Commission, by its orders dated 06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006,
consciously addressed these restrictions and relaxed them in favour of captive
and non-captive consumers of a Captive Power Plant (CPP). The relaxation was
twofold: (i) the contract demand could be reduced to any extent, even to zero, at
any time during the agreement period; and (ii) such reduction could be exercised
once in a year, as against the earlier stipulation of once in two years.
35. The expression “any time” employed in the Commission’s orders dated
06.02.2006 must be construed contextually. Its import is to lift the embargo
contained in Clause 7.9 ; namely, the prohibition against reduction within the initial
two-year period and the requirement of demonstrating compelling necessity to
the satisfaction of the licensee. In effect, captive consumers were conferred
liberty to reduce their contract demand at any stage of the agreement period,
without being fettered by the two-year bar or the requirement of proving
compelling reasons.
Page 15 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
36. We further note that the relaxation granted in the order dated 06.02.2006 is
in context of Clause 7.9 of supply code 2005 and there is no discussion/ reference
to procedure and time line prescribed in clause 7.11 of Supply Code 2005, while
granting such relaxation. Therefore, this relaxation pertains only to the
substantive restriction under Clause 7.9. It does not, by implication, extend to the
procedural framework and timelines prescribed under Clause 7.11. The
Commission’s orders are silent on Clause 7.11, and there is no indication that the
procedural safeguards such as the sixty-day period for disposal of applications,
the requirement of a reasoned speaking order, and the deemed permission
mechanism were intended to be dispensed with. To construe “any time” as
overriding Clause 7.11 would be to enlarge the scope of relaxation beyond its
expressed intent, and to dilute procedural safeguards which serve a vital
regulatory purpose, including procedural requirement, system load management,
and maintenance of grid stability.
37. Accordingly, in our view, while captive consumers enjoy substantive liberty
under Clause 7.9 as relaxed by the Commission, they remain bound by the
procedural discipline of Clause 7.11. The Appellant’s contention that the
concession of reduction to zero ipso facto altered the timeline under Clause 7.11
is unsustainable.
38. Further, we find merit in the submission of Respondents that the grant and
operationalizing of Open access from 04.11.2006 and reduction of contract
demand are two distinct activity and even if Open Access is operationalized from
04.11.2006, it would not mean automatic reduction in contract demand from that
date as open Access framework do not override the Supply Code. The Open
Access and contract demand are legally distinct. Open Access governs use of
Page 16 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
the distribution system, payment of surcharge/cross subsidy etc., whereas the
contract demand concerns the licensee's obligation to keep capacity available to
the consumer. The Discom could account for wheeled units under the open
Access, while billing on the subsisting contract demand of a consumer, until the
said contract demand is modified as per the supply code. Both the Open Access
and reduction of the contract demand are governed by the different framework
and the Open access framework do not override the Supply Code. Accordingly,
the contention of the Appellant that since open access has been made effective
from 04.11.2006, their contract demand should be considered as zero from
04.11.2006 has no merit The issue is, therefore, answered against the Appellant.
39. Accordingly, we hold that the relaxation granted by the State Commission
in its orders dated 06.02.2006 and 29.09.2006 was confined to the substantive
restriction under Clause 7.9 of the Supply Code, 2005, and did not extend to the
procedural framework and timelines prescribed under Clause 7.11 of supply Code
2005. The expression “any time” must be understood as lifting the embargo on
reduction of contract demand within the initial two-year period and dispensing
with the requirement of demonstrating compelling necessity, but not as overriding
the procedural discipline of Clause 7.11. In the present case, the Respondent–
CSPDCL has acted within the statutory framework by granting reduction with
effect from 01.01.2007, and the levy of demand charges for the intervening period
04.11.2006 to 31.12.2006 cannot be faulted.
40. In view of these observations, we do not feel it necessary to deliberate the
other contention of Appellant with regard to the action not being taken by
CSPDCL with regard to the signing of fresh agreement in terms of order dated
29.09.2006 as admittedly the contract demand of Appellant was reduced to Zero
Page 17 of 18

Judgement in Appeal No. 158 of 2016
w.e.f. 01.01.2007, within the time line stipulated in clause 7.11 of supply code
2005.
ORDER
In view of the above deliberations, we do not discern any infirmity in the Impugned
Order passed by the State Commission. The same is accordingly upheld. The
Captioned Appeal fails and is dismissed as being devoid of merit. Pending
interlocutory applications, if any, stand disposed of in terms of this judgment.
PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT ON THIS 19th DAY OF AUGUST, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson
